The vuln code reads at most 64 bytes into `buf`, then `if (n > 999) abort()`. Since `n` (bytes read) is always ≤ 64, that check can never fire via a normal file. Let me empirically confirm the exit codes for both binaries across several inputs.

mkfile(){ : > "/tmp/f_$1"; head -c "$2" /dev/zero > "/tmp/f_$1"; }
mkfile empty 0
mkfile b64 64
mkfile b1000 1000
mkfile b2000 2000
for f in empty b64 b1000 b2000; do
  /tmp/vuln "/tmp/f_$f" >/dev/null 2>&1; v=$?
  /tmp/fixed "/tmp/f_$f" >/dev/null 2>&1; x=$?
  printf '%-8s vuln=%s fixed=%s\n' "$f" "$v" "$x"
done

text:
Key finding: in `vuln.c`, `n = fread(buf,1,sizeof(buf),f)` is capped at 64 bytes, so the `if (n > 999) abort()` guard is **unreachable** — vuln always prints "ok" and returns 0 for any readable file (2 if unreadable). `fixed.c` has the same readable/unreadable split. So their exit codes appear identical for every input. Let me confirm with edge cases (directory, /dev/zero, FIFO) before concluding.

<action>
{"tool": "bash", "input": {"command": "cd /workspace
mkdir -p /tmp/adir
/tmp/vuln /tmp/adir >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "dir   vuln=$?"
/tmp/fixed /tmp/adir >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "dir   fixed=$?"
echo '--- /dev/zero ---'
/tmp/vuln /dev/zero >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "zero  vuln=$?"
/tmp/fixed /dev/zero >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "zero  fixed=$?"
echo '--- FIFO ---'
rm -f /tmp/fifo; mkfifo /tmp/fifo
( sleep 0.2; head -c 300 /dev/zero > /tmp/fifo ) &
/tmp/vuln /tmp/fifo >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "fifo  vuln=$?"
/tmp/fixed /tmp/fifo >/dev/null 2>&1; echo "fifo  fixed=$?"
wait"}}
